title.en: Product Architecture for AI Apps: Chat, Files, Tools, Memory, Evals

body.en:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

• Identify the core architectural components of a production-grade AI application
• Understand how chat interfaces, file handling, tool use, memory systems, and evaluation pipelines fit together
• Distinguish between stateless and stateful AI app designs
• Apply architectural thinking to plan a real-world AI product from the ground up

blocks.title: How to build AI-apps with React + FastAPI (full beginner tutorial)
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
A modern AI application is not just a wrapper around a language model. It is a layered system composed of several distinct architectural concerns.

The chat layer handles turn-based dialogue, routing user messages to the model and returning responses. The files layer manages document ingestion, chunking, embedding, and retrieval, enabling the model to reason over user-supplied content.

The tools layer exposes callable functions — such as web search, code execution, or database queries — that the model can invoke during inference. The memory layer persists context across sessions, combining short-term conversation history with long-term user profiles or knowledge stores.

Finally, the evals layer continuously measures model output quality, latency, cost, and safety, providing feedback loops that drive iteration. Together these five pillars form the backbone of any production AI product.

• Chat Layer: The conversational interface that manages turn sequencing, system prompts, and message routing between the user and the AI model.

• Tool Use (Function Calling): A mechanism that allows the model to request execution of predefined functions, extending its capabilities beyond text generation.

• Memory Architecture: The combination of in-context history, vector-based retrieval, and persistent user state that gives an AI app continuity across interactions.

• Evaluation Pipeline: An automated or semi-automated system that scores AI outputs on dimensions such as accuracy, helpfulness, latency, and safety to guide continuous improvement.

question.en: Which architectural layer is responsible for allowing a language model to execute a database query during a conversation?

text.en: Memory layer
Files layer
Tools layer
Evals layer

explanation.en: The tools layer exposes callable functions — including database queries, web searches, and code execution — that the model can invoke during inference via function calling mechanisms.

question.en: What is the primary purpose of the evals layer in an AI application architecture?

text.en: To store user conversation history across sessions
To continuously measure output quality, latency, cost, and safety
To chunk and embed documents for retrieval
To route messages from the user to the model

explanation.en: The evals layer is dedicated to measuring and monitoring AI outputs across multiple dimensions — quality, latency, cost, and safety — providing the feedback loops necessary for continuous product improvement.

question.en: Which of the following best describes a stateful AI application compared to a stateless one?

text.en: A stateful app processes each user message independently with no prior context
A stateful app relies solely on in-context window for all memory needs
A stateful app persists context, user profiles, and history across multiple sessions
A stateful app does not require a database or vector store

explanation.en: A stateful AI application persists conversation history, user profiles, and relevant context across sessions using memory systems such as databases and vector stores, enabling continuity and personalization.

body.en:
• A production AI app is a multi-layered system — chat, files, tools, memory, and evals — not simply a model API call.

• Each architectural layer addresses a distinct concern: interaction, knowledge, action, continuity, and quality assurance.

• Designing these layers explicitly from the start prevents technical debt and enables scalable, maintainable AI products.

Congratulations on completing Lesson 1: Product Architecture for AI Apps!

You now have a clear mental model of the five foundational pillars — chat, files, tools, memory, and evals — that define modern AI application architecture. This framework will serve as your reference point throughout the rest of this course and your career as a full-stack AI developer.

title.en: Provider Abstraction: Claude, OpenAI-Compatible APIs, Local Models, Fallback

body.en:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

• Explain why provider abstraction is essential in production AI applications
• Compare the Claude API, OpenAI-compatible APIs, and locally hosted models
• Design a provider abstraction layer that supports multiple backends
• Implement fallback and load-balancing strategies to improve reliability and cost efficiency

Hardcoding a single AI provider into your application creates fragility. Providers change pricing, introduce rate limits, experience outages, and evolve their APIs. A robust AI backend abstracts the provider behind a unified interface.

Anthropic's Claude API offers strong reasoning and long context windows with a distinct message format. OpenAI-compatible APIs — including OpenAI itself, Azure OpenAI, Together AI, and Groq — share a common chat completions schema, simplifying multi-provider support. Local models served via tools like Ollama or vLLM expose the same OpenAI-compatible interface, enabling on-premise deployments.

A well-designed abstraction layer maps provider-specific request and response shapes to a canonical internal format. Fallback logic routes requests to a secondary provider when the primary fails or rate-limits. Cost-aware routing can preferentially select cheaper models for simpler tasks. This architecture dramatically improves resilience, flexibility, and cost control.

blocks.title: Learn AI Engineering in 2026 | Build a Full Stack AI Websites with Agents
blocks.label: Recommended Viewing

body.en:
• Provider Abstraction Layer: An interface or adapter pattern that normalizes requests and responses across different AI provider APIs, decoupling application logic from any specific vendor.

• OpenAI-Compatible API: A widely adopted REST API schema for chat completions that has become a de facto standard, implemented by many providers and local model servers.

• Fallback Strategy: Logic that automatically retries a failed request against one or more alternative providers, maintaining service availability during outages or rate-limit events.

• Cost-Aware Routing: A dispatch mechanism that selects the most cost-effective model capable of handling a given request, optimizing inference spend without sacrificing quality.

question.en: What is the main benefit of implementing a provider abstraction layer in an AI application?

text.en: It increases the number of tokens sent per request
It locks the application to the best-performing provider
It decouples application logic from specific vendor APIs, improving resilience and flexibility
It removes the need for authentication credentials

explanation.en: A provider abstraction layer normalizes the interface to multiple AI backends, allowing the application to switch providers, add fallbacks, or adjust routing without changing core business logic.

question.en: Which of the following tools exposes locally hosted models via an OpenAI-compatible API?

text.en: Pinecone
Ollama
LangSmith
Supabase

explanation.en: Ollama is a popular tool for running large language models locally. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint, making it easy to integrate into applications that already support the OpenAI API schema.

question.en: In a cost-aware routing strategy, how are requests typically dispatched?

text.en: All requests are always sent to the most capable and expensive model available
Requests are routed randomly across all configured providers
Requests are sent to the most cost-effective model that can adequately handle the task
Requests are batched and sent to a single provider at scheduled intervals

explanation.en: Cost-aware routing evaluates the complexity or requirements of each request and dispatches it to the cheapest model that meets those requirements, reducing inference costs while maintaining acceptable output quality.

body.en:
• Never hardcode a single AI provider; always design a provider abstraction layer to future-proof your application against vendor changes and outages.

• The OpenAI-compatible API schema has become a de facto standard, enabling a single client implementation to communicate with multiple providers and local models.

• Combining fallback strategies with cost-aware routing yields an AI backend that is simultaneously more reliable, more flexible, and more economical.

Congratulations on completing Lesson 2: Provider Abstraction!

You now understand how to architect a model-agnostic AI backend that can seamlessly switch between Claude, OpenAI-compatible services, and local models — with intelligent fallback and cost-aware routing built in.

In Lesson 3, we shift focus to the user experience side of AI applications, exploring streaming responses and the full response lifecycle.

body.en:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

• Explain how server-sent events and token streaming work in AI applications
• Describe the full lifecycle of an AI response from request initiation to completion
• Implement graceful handling of partial responses, errors, and interruptions
• Apply streaming UX best practices to improve perceived performance and user satisfaction

title.en: Streaming UX and the AI Response Lifecycle

body.en:
Language models generate text token by token. Waiting for the full response before rendering it creates a poor user experience, especially for long outputs. Streaming solves this by delivering tokens to the client as they are produced.

The standard mechanism is Server-Sent Events (SSE), an HTTP protocol that keeps a connection open and pushes incremental data chunks from server to client. The response lifecycle begins when the client sends a request, transitions through a connecting state, then enters the streaming state as tokens arrive, and finally reaches completion when the model emits a stop token or finish signal.

Handling this lifecycle robustly requires managing: the loading state before the first token arrives, graceful rendering of partial markdown or code, error states for network interruptions or provider errors, and cancellation — allowing users to stop generation mid-stream. Each of these states must be reflected in the UI to build a trustworthy, responsive AI product.

• Server-Sent Events (SSE): A unidirectional HTTP streaming protocol used to push incremental data — such as tokens — from server to client over a persistent connection.

• Time to First Token (TTFT): A critical latency metric measuring the elapsed time between sending a request and receiving the first token, directly impacting perceived responsiveness.

• Graceful Degradation: The practice of handling partial, interrupted, or erroneous streaming responses in a way that preserves UI stability and informs the user without crashing.

• Cancellation and Abort: The ability for a user or system to terminate an in-progress generation, requiring proper cleanup of server-side resources and client-side state.

question.en: What HTTP mechanism is most commonly used to deliver streaming AI responses from server to client?

text.en: WebSockets with binary frames
Long polling with JSON payloads
Server-Sent Events (SSE)
GraphQL subscriptions

explanation.en: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is the standard mechanism for AI token streaming. It uses a persistent HTTP connection to push incremental text chunks from the server to the client as they are generated by the model.

question.en: What does Time to First Token (TTFT) measure?

text.en: The total duration of a complete model response
The time between sending a request and receiving the first streamed token
The number of tokens generated per second by the model
The latency of the database query before model inference begins

explanation.en: TTFT (Time to First Token) measures the elapsed time from when a request is sent until the first token is received from the model. It is a key UX metric because users perceive the app as responsive as soon as text begins appearing.

question.en: When a user clicks 'Stop' to cancel an in-progress AI generation, which of the following is the correct behavior?

text.en: The client should wait for the full response before discarding it
The client should abort the request and the server should release associated resources
The server should continue generating and cache the result for later
The UI should freeze until the current token is fully rendered

explanation.en: Proper cancellation requires the client to abort the fetch or SSE connection and the server to detect the disconnection and stop inference, releasing compute and memory resources promptly.

body.en:
• Streaming via Server-Sent Events dramatically improves perceived performance by displaying tokens as they are generated rather than waiting for the full response.

• The AI response lifecycle includes distinct states — connecting, streaming, complete, error, and cancelled — each requiring explicit handling in both backend and frontend code.

• Time to First Token (TTFT) is the most user-impactful latency metric in AI applications and should be monitored and optimized as a primary engineering concern.

Congratulations on completing Lesson 3: Streaming UX and Response Lifecycle!

You now understand how to deliver a fast, resilient, and user-friendly AI chat experience using token streaming, SSE, and robust lifecycle state management.

title.en: Data Model for Users, Conversations, Messages, and Artifacts

body.en:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

• Design a relational data model that supports multi-user AI applications at scale
• Define the relationships between users, conversations, messages, and artifacts
• Apply best practices for storing message roles, metadata, and token counts
• Plan schema strategies for artifacts such as generated files, code, and images

A well-designed data model is the foundation of a scalable AI application. At its core, four entities drive the schema: Users, Conversations, Messages, and Artifacts.

The Users table stores identity, authentication tokens, preferences, and usage quotas. Each user can own many Conversations — a Conversation groups a sequence of messages under a shared context, storing metadata like title, model selection, system prompt, and timestamps.

Messages belong to a Conversation and carry a role field (system, user, or assistant), a content field, token counts for cost tracking, and ordering metadata. Artifacts are discrete outputs — generated images, code files, documents, or structured data — linked to the message that produced them and stored with their MIME type, size, and storage URL.

Indexing strategy matters: conversations should be indexed by user and updated_at for fast inbox queries; messages by conversation_id and sequence for efficient history retrieval. Soft deletes preserve audit trails without losing context.

• Message Role: A field on each message record that identifies its sender type — 'system' for instructions, 'user' for human input, and 'assistant' for model output — following the standard chat completions schema.

• Conversation Context: The aggregated, ordered sequence of messages associated with a single conversation thread, reconstructed from the database and passed as context to the model on each turn.

• Artifact: A discrete, addressable output object — such as a generated image, code file, or document — stored separately from message text and linked by foreign key to its originating message.

• Token Accounting: The practice of recording input and output token counts on each message row to enable accurate cost attribution, quota enforcement, and usage analytics per user or conversation.

question.en: Which message role should be used to provide persistent instructions to the model that govern its behavior throughout a conversation?

text.en: user
assistant
system
context

explanation.en: The 'system' role is used for messages that set the model's behavior, persona, and constraints. System messages are typically placed at the start of the conversation context and apply throughout the entire interaction.

question.en: Why is it important to store token counts on each message record in the database?

text.en: Token counts determine the display font size in the chat UI
Token counts enable cost attribution, quota enforcement, and usage analytics
Token counts are required by all AI provider APIs before a request can be made
Token counts replace the need for message timestamps

explanation.en: Storing token counts per message allows the application to calculate per-user or per-conversation inference costs, enforce usage quotas, and provide detailed analytics dashboards — all essential for operating a production AI service.

question.en: How should a generated image produced during an AI conversation be stored in the data model?

text.en: Encoded as a base64 string inside the message content field
As a separate Artifact record linked by foreign key to the originating message, with a storage URL and MIME type
As a new User record with image metadata attached
Stored only in the client browser cache and never persisted server-side

explanation.en: Artifacts such as generated images should be stored as separate records in an Artifacts table, linked to the message that produced them via a foreign key. This keeps message records lightweight and allows artifacts to be independently managed, versioned, and accessed.

body.en:
• The core data model of an AI application revolves around four entities — Users, Conversations, Messages, and Artifacts — each with clearly defined relationships and indexed access patterns.

• Message roles (system, user, assistant) are not just API conventions; they should be persisted in the database to faithfully reconstruct conversation context for each model turn.

• Artifacts should be stored as first-class entities separate from message text, enabling independent management, retrieval, and versioning of generated content.

Congratulations on completing Lesson 4: Data Model for Users, Conversations, Messages, and Artifacts!

You now have the knowledge to design a robust, scalable database schema that underpins a production AI application — from user identity and conversation threads to message history and generated artifacts.

You have completed all four lessons of Modern AI App Foundations. Proceed to the course lab to apply everything you have learned by drawing and documenting a complete, deployable AI application architecture.
